title: Formulae for Focal Lengths in Geometrical Optics
short_intro: The focal length of an optical system is determined by its radii of curvature, refractive index, and the surrounding medium according to rigorous geometrical optics principles. These formulations govern the convergence and divergence properties of thin and thick lenses as well as spherical mirrors.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Lens Maker's Formula, mirror formula, magnification, simple combination of thin lenses in contact, sign convention.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Lenses separated by a distance, equivalent focal length, focal length of systems with varying refractive indices, displacement method for finding focal length.

prerequisites: Laws of refraction and Snell's Law
Cartesian sign convention for spherical surfaces

concept_notes.heading: Lens Maker's Formula
bullets: Relates the focal length (f) of a thin lens to the relative refractive index (μ) and the radii of curvature (R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>) of its two surfaces.
Derived by applying refraction successively at two spherical boundaries assuming a paraxial ray tracing approach.
Depends directly on the ratio of the refractive index of the lens material to that of the surrounding medium.

concept_notes.heading: Spherical Mirror Focal Length
bullets: The focal length of a spherical mirror is strictly half of its radius of curvature under paraxial conditions: f = R / 2.
Independent of the surrounding medium because reflection does not depend on the speed of light in the medium.
Concave mirrors possess negative focal lengths while convex mirrors possess positive focal lengths in standard Cartesian sign conventions.

concept_notes.heading: Combination of Thin Lenses
bullets: When two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> are placed in close contact, the reciprocal of the equivalent focal length is the algebraic sum of their individual reciprocals.
The total power of a combination of lenses in contact is given by the algebraic sum of the individual powers: P = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub>.
Useful for designing achromatic doublets and estimating cumulative optical convergence.

concept_notes.heading: Displacement Method (U-V Method)
bullets: An experimental method to determine the focal length of a convex lens using an object-screen distance greater than 4f.
Yields two distinct positions of the lens for which a sharp image is formed on the fixed screen.
Provides an accurate estimation of focal length without directly measuring object and image distances from the optical center.

derivations.title: Lens Maker's Formula Derivation
derivations.conditions: Thin lens in a medium, paraxial rays, spherical surfaces of radii R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>
steps: Apply refraction formula for the first spherical surface separating media of refractive index n<sub>1</sub> and n<sub>2</sub>: \frac{n_2}{v_1} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R_1}
For the second surface, the image formed by the first surface acts as a virtual object, with refraction from n<sub>2</sub> to n<sub>1</sub>: \frac{n_1}{v} - \frac{n_2}{v_1} = \frac{n_1 - n_2}{R_2}

Adding both equations eliminates the intermediate image distance v<sub>1</sub> and yields the general thin lens formula: \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = (\frac{n_2}{n_1} - 1)(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2})

derivations.title: Equivalent Focal Length of Two Thin Lenses Separated by Distance d
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> separated by a distance d in air
steps: Trace a paraxial ray parallel to the principal axis at height h<sub>1</sub> incident on the first lens.
Determine the deviation and the height h<sub>2</sub> at which the ray strikes the second lens: h_2 = h_1 (1 - \frac{d}{f_1})
Calculate the total deviation produced by the system to find the reciprocal of the equivalent focal length F.

graphs_and_experiments.title: u-v Graph for a Convex Lens
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A hyperbola plot of image distance v versus object distance u, or a plot of 1/v versus 1/u yielding a straight line with intercepts equal to 1/f.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The straight-line plot of 1/v versus 1/u has a slope of +1 and intercepts on both axes equal to 1/f.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually for slope interpretation and graphical determination of focal length.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement Method Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_drag: Graph of magnification versus lens displacement or object-screen distance L versus lens separation d.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Allows precise calculation of focal length f without locating the optical center directly.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems based on the formula f = (L<sup>2</sup> - d<sup>2</sup>)/4L.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of Focal Length with Wavelength (Chromatic Aberration)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of focal length f versus wavelength λ showing decrease of focal length toward the violet end of the spectrum.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Refractive index depends on wavelength (μ ∝ 1/λ<sup>2</sup> via Cauchy's relation), causing shorter wavelengths to focus closer to the lens.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on chromatic aberration and dispersive power.

solved_numericals.question: A double convex lens has radii of curvature of 20 cm each. If the refractive index of the glass is 1.5, calculate its focal length in air.
solution_steps: Identify given values: R_1 = +20 cm, R_2 = -20 cm, μ = 1.5.
Substitute values into the Lens Maker's Formula: \frac{1}{f} = (1.5 - 1) \left(\frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{-20}\right).

solved_numericals.question: Two thin lenses of focal lengths +20 cm and -30 cm are placed in contact. Find the focal length and power of the combination.
solution_steps: Identify given values: f_1 = +20 cm = 0.2 m, f_2 = -30 cm = -0.3 m.
Calculate power: P = \frac{1}{F (in m)} = \frac{1}{0.6} D = +1.67 D.

solved_numericals.question: A convex lens of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of 20 cm in air. What will be its focal length when immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.33?
solution_steps: Use the lens focal length ratio formula: \frac{f_m}{f_a} = \frac{(n_g - 1)}{\left(\frac{n_g}{n_m} - 1\right)}.
Substitute values: n_g = 1.5, n_m = 1.33 = \frac{4}{3}, f_a = 20 cm.

assumptions_and_limitations: Paraxial ray approximation is assumed, which limits validity to small angles of incidence where sin(θ) ≈ θ.
Lenses are considered thin, meaning thickness is neglected compared to radii of curvature and object/image distances.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The focal length of a lens changes when it is inverted.
common_misconceptions.correct: The focal length remains exactly the same upon inversion.
common_misconceptions.why: Focal length depends only on the radii of curvature and refractive indices, which do not change when the lens is flipped.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A convex lens always converges light regardless of the surrounding medium.
common_misconceptions.correct: A convex lens can behave as a diverging lens if immersed in a medium with a higher refractive index than the lens material.
common_misconceptions.why: The relative refractive index term (μ<sub>rel</sub> - 1) becomes negative, reversing the optical action.
